html:
A ring of great standing stones on Salisbury Plain in southern England, built in stages between about 3000 and 1500 BCE by farming peoples who left no writing.

It began as a round ditch and bank, used for cremation burials. About 2500 BCE the builders raised the large stones:

  • the sarsens, sandstone blocks of up to 25 tonnes, dragged about 25 km from the north and set as a circle of uprights capped by lintels, with five taller arches inside;
  • the bluestones, smaller stones of about 2 tonnes each, brought some 240 km from the Preseli Hills in west Wales.

The stones were shaped and jointed like timber, with pegs and sockets. The whole design lines up with sunrise at midsummer and sunset at midwinter. What it was for is still argued: a place for the dead, a calendar of the seasons, a gathering point for scattered communities, or all three.
sum: A ring of great standing stones on Salisbury Plain in southern England, built in stages between about 3000 and 1500 BCE by farming peoples who left no writing.
